the walls surrounding the town were built between the end of the 13th century and the 1330s. the town’s defence system was strengthened by several towers and the three gates mentioned above. From the first half of the 14th century, it was closely linked to the cathedral and the chapter castle, which provided shelter for the townspeople in times of danger. Communication-wise, the most important gates were the Malborska Gate (Marienburger tor), which led to northern Pomesania and on to Malbork, and the Grudziądzka Gate (Graudenzer tor), also called the High Gate (Hohe tor), which led south to Chełmno Land. two defensive towers were erected on either side of the Malborska Gate. the Grudziądzka Gate was protected by a defensive foreground. Behind the Nizinna Gate (Lowland Gate), also known as the Water Gate (German: Wasser tor) in the 16th century, and as the Gniewska Gate (Mewer tor) in the 18th century, there was a road to the Kwidzyn Valley and to the Vistula crossing. the fourth gate was located in the north-western corner of the town walls, but was removed at the beginning of the 14th century after the construction of the chapter castle, to which the northern edge of the western section of the town walls adjoined. In the second half of the 17th century, the town’s defence system was strengthened by the construction of masonry bastions in front of the Grudziądzka and Malborska gates. In the 18th century, as part of the modernisation of the spatial layout, all gates were demolished. the earliest to be demolished was the Nizinna Gate, between 1743 and 1755 it was followed by the Malborska Gate, and in 1758 by the Grudziądzka Gate38 the town hall, situated in the middle of the market square, was the oldest public building in Kwidzyn. In the pre-industrial era, fires posed the greatest threat to the buildings, which were constructed mainly of wood. It should be emphasised that the post-fire reconstructions of the town did not change the spatial layout. In the Middle Ages, towns were destroyed by fire mainly during wars. In 1414, the burghers themselves set fire to their houses to make it difficult for Polish troops to storm the chapter’s castle. Fires also destroyed the town during the thirteen years’ War in 1460 and during the War of the Priests in 1478. In the early modern period, the most extensive damage was caused by a fire in 1710, which destroyed a third of the town’s buildings, including the eastern part of the market square, Szeroka Street and the Grudziądzkie Suburb57 Estimates of the number of inhabitants of Kwidzyn in the medieval and modern periods can only be based on indirect indicators such as the number of properties and the number of households. In legal terms, the population of Kwidzyn was divided into three groups. the highest place in the social and property hierarchy was occupied by full burghers (German: Vollbürger). they owned plots of land with the right to brew beer, as well as fields, gardens and pastures within the land patrimony. Members of this group also enjoyed the right to trade and to be on the town council. Full burghership could be granted to free persons who could produce a letter of good birth stating that they are the offspring of a legitimate union. From the 16th century onwards, the nobility were exempted from the requirement to present these certificates. Entry into the burghership registry also required payment of a fee and the possession of appropriate arms. In the 18th century, we observe a process where the ownership of a property was no longer a requirement in order to obtain full burghership. the town council could also grant full burghership to the person renting the house, who could not, however, enjoy the privilege of brewing beer59. the second group consisted of burghers with so-called lesser burghership. As a rule, they lived in shacks for which they paid rent to the town treasury. they also had to pay fees for the use of pastures and forests. the lowest place in the social hierarchy was occupied by residents without municipal rights: hired labourers, servants, marginal social groups and hortulanii (similar to cotters). Based on sources from the first half of the 18th century, it can be estimated that full burghers and their families made up about 39%, lesser burghers 11% and remaining residents 50% of the town population60 the inhabitants of Kwidzyn, like the entire population of Prussia in the Middle Ages and in the early modern period, were characterised by a diverse ethnic structure. the most numerous group was made up of burghers of German origin. People bearing surnames indicating Polish origin in the 15th century were occasionally mentioned among members of the town council and as property owners. the oldest town book of 1480 also records several inhabitants of Prussian origin. the 1480 and 1586 willkurs contain records prohibiting the granting of citizenship to Poles and their admission to guilds controlling food production. the phenomenon of this grassroots restriction of access to municipal law for the Polish population was mainly due to the desire to protect urban economic resources, threatened in times of crisis, from competition. there were no such impediments to Poles having sufficient financial resources enabling them to build a house on an undeveloped plot of land. the presence of the Polish population in early modern Kwidzyn is evidenced by their use of the eastern part of the Protestant cathedral, which was called the Polish church61. the western part of the cathedral was used in 1549–1574 by the unity of the Brethren, who were invited to Kwidzyn and other Prussian towns by the second Lutheran bishop of Pomesania, Paul Speratus. the newcomers took up residence in shacks on Wąska Street. they also asked the Prussian duke to give them about 20 empty, full-size plots of land, which the local burghers refused to build on. Due to resistance of the Kwidzyn burghers, this wish was not fulfilled and only few members of the unity of the Brethren received the abandoned plots of land from the duke. Difficult material circumstances and attempts to subordinate the Brethren to the town’s Evangelical church forced most of them to leave Prussia around 157462

In terms of economy, pre-industrial Kwidzyn developed similar to other small towns in Central and Eastern Europe, whose trade, production and service functions were oriented towards the immediate surroundings and agriculture was an indispensable element of urban life. the residents of Kwidzyn were involved in the Vistula trade through the harbour in Korzeniewo. the local skippers were members of the brotherhood of the Vistula skippers from the 1490s and, according to the 1480 willkur, held a monopoly on transporting goods to the town harbour, as foreign ships were prohibited from coming to the harbour without the permission of the town council. It was not until 1575 that the Prussian nobility received permission from the duke to export goods freely through the harbour at Korzeniewo, but with the obligation to pay a fee to the town council. Grain predominated among the exported goods. A lesser role was played by forestry goods (wood, tar, pitch), meat, and products of local crafts65 fairs organised in Kwidzyn had a regional scope. the oldest one is mentioned in the 1390s; it was held in autumn and attended by merchants from Gdańsk. It ranged from daily sales at the bread, butchers’ and shoemakers’ benches and stallholders’ stalls by the town hall to weekly markets, which were the primary form of commercial contact with the people living in the surrounding villages67 All house owners in Kwidzyn were also farmers, as each plot of land had fields and meadows assigned to it in the Kwidzyn Lowlands and the upland area. the importance of agriculture to the town’s economy is evidenced by the council’s efforts to enlarge the land patrimony on the upland from the beginning of the 16th century, mentioned above. Citizens farmed their land with their own equipment, but most often employed servants or tenants (cotters), who received a piece of land as remuneration. With the permission of the town council, citizens’ fields could have been leased in return for rent. the town council organised joint grazing of the animals reared by burghers. In 1572, the town shepherds grazed 530 horses, 820 cattle, 740 pigs and 432 sheep. the wealthiest citizens owned several dozen head of livestock, while those living in sheds and hired labourers usually kept one or two cows and a few pigs68 In the Middle Ages, Kwidzyn formed part of the Pomesanian diocese. It is likely that the parish of Kwidzyn was established soon after the reconstruction of the town began in the 1270s. the first parish priest of Kwidzyn is referenced in 1286. In that year, the right of advowson over the parish church was handed over to the chapter by bishop Albert69. Erected on the basis of a parish church, the Cathedral of the Blessed Virgin Mary and St. John the Evangelist was not only the main church of the diocese, but also provided pastoral care for the inhabitants of the town and its land patrimony. In the late 14th and early 15th centuries, the Pomesanian chapter succeeded in expanding the religious potential of the cathedral on a scale beyond the borders of episcopal Pomesania. of major importance in this process was the cult of St. John the Evangelist and the efforts made by the chapter to canonise Dorothea of Mątowy, a mystic from Gdansk who, at her own request, was walled up in a cell in the cathedral, where she died on 25 June 139470. the sacral topography of Kwidzyn in the Middle Ages was complemented by two hospitals. In the 14th century, the chapter founded the hospital of the Holy Spirit in front of the Malborska Gate. the town founded the hospital of St. George located in front of the Grudziądzka Gate71. As Bishop Erhard von Queiß adopted the Protestant denomination and the chapter was dissolved in 1527, the sacral topography of Kwidzyn underwent significant changes. the cathedral became a Protestant church, with separate liturgical spaces designated for the German and Polish populations,

the first Partition of Poland presented Kwidzyn with a great opportunity for development. Despite strenuous diplomatic efforts by King Frederick II of Prussia and the exertion of various forms of pressure aimed at inducing toruń and Gdańsk to voluntarily submit to the Kingdom of Prussia, these cities were not incorporated into the Prussian state during the first Partition of Poland in 1772. the Prussian monarch took advantage of the Kwidzyn’s potential and its location by deciding to open there a customs chamber as early as March 1765 under the pretext that the Polish Sejm had passed a general duty on goods floated down the Vistula. the chamber collected a high transit duty on goods transported by river in both directions between toruń and Gdańsk74. the ruler’s policy was to force toruń merchants to sell grain at low prices to the Prussian state warehouses in Kwidzyn. In April 1772, i.e. 4 months before the partition treaty of the three powers, Frederick II officially or- dered that 1/3 of the cargo of grain transported by the Vistula be sold in Kwidzyn at prices far below market prices75 After the first Partition of Poland, there was a need for new administrative divisions. As a result, Kwidzyn gained in importance and became the capital of the newly created West Prussian Province (German: Provinz Westpreußen) with the seat of its authorities. By placing the regional capital in Kwidzyn, account was taken of the town’s convenient postal connection to Berlin, as well as the building substance left behind by russian troops, which resided in Kwidzyn: former residence of General Fermor was reused by Prussian officials. A decree of 28 September 1772 established a Higher State Court for the areas administered from Kwidzyn and, on 3 November, a Chamber of War and Domain Affairs (Kriegsund Domänenkammer), which did not report to the General Directorate in Berlin but directly to King frederick II76. the end of 1808 brought changes to the state administration. A new office, the Kwidzyn Governmental District (Wespreussische regierung zu Marienwerder), with the authority of a super-president, replaced the Chamber of War and Domain Affairs. After Napoleon’s defeat in 1815, Danzig became the capital of the West Prussian Province, but Kwidzyn, as the capital of the Governmental District, retained its importance. the area administered by the Kwidzyn authorities totalled approximately 17,595 km² (318 square miles). the maximum extent of the Kwidzyn Governmental District from north to south amounted to about 14 Prussian miles and from west to east to 41 Prussian miles. the part lying on the right side of the Vistula river occupied about 1/3 of the total area.

During the French-Prussian wars, Kwidzyn became a war base, mainly because of the crossing on the Vistula river, built in Korzeniewo for the troops advancing to Moscow. An undoubted shock for the inhabitants of Kwidzyn was the defeat of Prussia in the 1806–1807 war with France. At the beginning of 1807, the war reached the town and on 30 January 1807, French troops entered Kwidzyn. Marshal François Joseph Lefebvre set up his quarters and a large military hospital in Kwidzyn. the French had no regard for the needs of the inhabitants, demanding high contributions and requisitioning lodgings. the Prussian army returned to Kwidzyn in December 1807 as a result of the Treaty of Tilsit77. From 1810, General Hans David Ludwig Graf york von Wartenburg, commander-in-chief of the Prussian reinforcement corps during Napoleon’s invasion of russia, had his quarters in the horse stable next to the cathedral. It was thanks to Graf york that a military convention was signed in tauragė on 30 December 1812, under which the Prussian army, at that time at Napoleon’s side, changed sides and allied with russia. At the turn of 1812 and 1813, the defeated French army, crossed the Vistula heading west. Numerous russian troops also marched through the town. unfortunately, Napoleon’s soldiers 72 A. In terms of communication, the town was strongly influenced by its geographical location. the main role in the 18th and 19th century was definitely played by the Vistula river, which “cut off ” communication with the western part of the Governmental District; in addition, Kwidzyn was several kilometres away from the Vistula. therefore, the town was adversely affected by such investments as the extension of roads between Bydgoszcz and Gdańsk to the west of the Vistula, or the ferry connection in Korzeniewo, which depended on the seasons and floods. the construction of the road to Malbork was completed in 1847, to Prabuty in 1857, and southwards to Grudziądz only in 1864. railway communication was in worse condition. Neither the Bydgoszcz–Gdańsk Eastern railway, nor the line to Königsberg with railway bridges near tczew, the Vistula crossing completed in 1857, and the Nogat river bridge crossing near Malbork ran through the town. the Malbork–Mława line also omitted Kwidzyn. It was not until the construction of the Vistula railway in 1883 that the town was connected to the railway via the toruń–Malbork route. the construction of further lines, Kisielice–Kwidzyn in 1900, and especially Smętowo–Prabuty in 1909, improved the situation by creating a direct connection between the town and the main transport routes in the region80 In 1900, the construction of a beautiful neo-Gothic railway station building was completed. the most notable change was the construction of a rail-road bridge over the Vistula between Grabowo and opaleń in 1909, connecting the town with the western part of the Governmental District. the construction of the first railway line and the rebuilding of the tracks for subsequent rail connections irrevocably divided the town into two parts. the terrain required the tracks to be laid in a ravine, and the two parts of the town were joined by a series of viaducts. 78 P. A huge barracks complex of the Non-Commissioned officer School (Königliche unteroffiziersschule) was built between today’s Grudziądzka and 11 Listopada streets. Horses continued to be the main mode of transport. the royal horse stud, which operated at the castle, in the very centre of the town, was given a new location due to severely limited expansion possibilities and the need for extensive renovation. In 1910, after several years of construction, the stud was moved to Miłosna (Liebenthal) near the forest area, where an enclosed complex of huge stables was built, with an indoor riding school, a water tower with a windmill, and a residential area for the workers87. the stud operated here until 1945, when the horses and equipment were evacuated deep into Germany.

Kwidzyn was still the seat of authorities of the Governmental District and the Higher State Court (oberlandesgericht). the town’s favourable economic condition was evidenced by investments made by the town and district authorities. one of such investments was the construction of a new post office building between 1911 and 1913 in neo-Gothic style, and the building of the landrat officer (Kreishaus) in 1915 on Warszawska Street, which besides offices and a meeting room also housed the landrat officer’s flat. A very beneficial decision for the town was the purchase of the gasworks from Aktienge- sellschaft für Gas-und Elektrizität, the investment in improving the electricity supply, the renewal of the water supply wells. At the time when Prussia seized the Polish lands, Kwidzyn was a small town with a population of no more than 2,800. From 1774, planned colonisation began. the Prussian ruler Frederick wanted some migrants to settle in the towns. As many as 51 families settled in Kwidzyn. In 1782, settlers from Württemberg and Baden also arrived in the Kwidzyn department, with 5 families coming to the town89. this coincided with an influx of officials. In the first ten years, the town’s population increased by one thousand people. However, an analysis of population growth shows that this was not an intensive influx (see table 2), but rather a moderate one, between 1.2% and 2.5% per year90. Nevertheless, the very fact that the provincial government was located in a small agrarian Prussian town resulted in an acute housing famine and the need to expand the town. the character of Kwidzyn as an important administrative centre was already very clearly established. Government officials, together with their families, accounted for about a third of Kwidzyn’s total population. In 1838, there were 351 officials in the town, whose overall population was 4,936. Following the changes, on 1 January 1999 Kwidzyn again became the seat of a poviat and was incorporated into the Pomeranian Voivodeship, as decided under the new reform of the administrative division of Poland introducing a three-tier structure of territorial division127 Although no battles were fought in Kwidzyn during the Second World War, the town suffered huge losses in buildings. In December 2016, the last remaining original townhouse in the vicinity of the castle was demolished. the town as the investor decided that it was not possible to integrate the building into the second quarter of the reconstruction. In the second half of 2017, the reconstruction of the second quarter of the old town, also designed as a single block, began. As before, the shape and appearance was the outcome of an earlier architectural competition. Construction was completed in 2020.

one of the key undertakings of the 1970s became the construction of a cellulose and paper factory (Zakłady Celulozo-Papierowe – ZCP, also referred to as “Celuloza”) started in 1972. this investment was one of the largest in the period of the Polish People’s republic. the goal of bringing the cellulose and paper industry into the town was to create additional jobs for the residents of Kwidzyn and a decisive development of the town’s infrastructure. unfortunately, the process of establishing the factory lasted more than 10 years, consuming huge financial resources and facing difficulties and interruptions. It was not until 22 November 1981 that ZCP managed to produce the first batch of cellulose, and between 1985 and 1989 specialised paper 140 J Kluczkowski, Starówka przed odbudową, “Kurier Kwidzyński” 11/402 (1999), p. 8. 141 R cybulski, Jest zezwolenie na odbudowę starówki, source: portal Kwidzyn naszemiasto.pl http://kwidzyn.naszemiasto.pl/archiwum/1443376,kwidzyn -jest-zezwolenie-na-odbudowe-starowki,id,t.html machines were put into operation. on 2 January 1992, ZCP was transformed into a sole shareholder Joint Stock Company of the State treasury, and on 10 August 1992, 80% of ZCP’s shares were sold to the American company International Paper. the remaining 20% of shares were divided among the 4,000 employees of the factory, who then resold them to International Paper. Currently (as of 2021), it is a factory owned by the Austrian Mayr-Melnhof Group (MM Kwidzyn). Along with the project to build ZCP, the Council of Ministers adopted projects on so-called “accompanying investments”, including the construction of two schools, two kindergartens, a nursery, a medical clinic, the modernisation of streets, a heating collector and a bus station in Kwidzyn. Changes related to the administrative reform, the construction of ZCP and the increase in the number of inhabitants also caused a breakthrough in Kwidzyn’s communication. In 1975, town buses entered the streets of Kwidzyn, initially running only between ZCP and the town, transporting “Celuloza” employees to work. Previously, the only form of public transport were taxis142 the construction of ZCP had an almost revolutionary effect on the character of Kwidzyn as a town. Within four years (1976–1980), the population increased by 4,000 people, reaching 32,000. Apart from the huge paper factory, in the 1970s and 1980s Kwidzyn was also home to other enterprises, such as Warmian fruit and vegetable processing factory (Warmińskie Zakłady Przetwórstwa owocowo-Warzywnego – WZPoW), “Polmo” automotive electrotechnics (Zakłady Elektrotechniki Motoryzacyjnej “Polmo”) or workers’ cooperatives named “Meblos” and “Powiśle”, employing a total of over a thousand people and turning Kwidzyn into an industrial town143. Since the late 1990s, Large industrial plants such as MM – Kwidzyn, Jabil Circuit Poland, Lacroix Electronics, Plati Polska, LEMAHIEu Polska, Knauf Pack, Pamapol S.A. or Zieliński meat processing plant have started operating in Kwidzyn. the town is becoming a leader not only in paper production, but also in the electronics industry.

the end of the Second World War brought a radical change to Kwidzyn’s situation due to the almost complete replacement of the population. As a result of the evacuation ordered by the German authorities in January 1945, 99% of the inhabitants left their hometown within a few days. From the early spring of 1945, new residents began to arrive in Kwidzyn. the most numerous group were people displaced from central Poland, Grudziądz and Warsaw. the second group were repatriates, today also called Kresowians, who settled individually, but also as families, neighbours or even entire villages. It could have helped them settle more easily in a new place, as it gave them a greater sense of security and the opportunity to support each other. there was still a group of indigenous Kwidzyn inhabitants – Germans and people with German citizenship. the reason for their continued presence in the town was that they did not manage to 142 Z. Girzyński, K. Nawrocki, Kwidzyn 1975–1990 (as n. 138), p. 481. 143 Ibidem, p. 470. evacuate or made an attempt to return to their homes after the war. By the end of 1949, they had mostly left the town forever. the first registration records in the town were kept from 2 April 1945. originally they were kept in a book system. regular population records in the card system began to be kept from 22 September 1945144. Poland’s first general population census was carried out on 14 February 1946. the population of Kwidzyn amounted to 7,986 people, including 4437 women and 3549 men. the number of children and adolescents under 18 years of age was 2,898145. However, the population structure of the town was undergoing dynamic changes. the displacement of the German population (who returned to the town after the evacuation in January) and the influx of the Polish population continued, although some decided to move again. In october 1946, the Municipal Council of Kwidzyn reported that 316 Germans were present in the town146. As a result of the action of the ultimate displacement of Germans, completed in october 1948, and the settlement of Poles mainly from the Eastern Borderlands, Grudziądz, Warsaw and central Poland, in 1950 there were almost 13,500 people living in Kwidzyn147. Between the censuses of 1950 and 1960, the population of Kwidzyn increased by almost 60% to 20,197 people. During this period, some of the inhabitants left the town and went to the West Germany or East Germany, within the family reunification action. For example, in 1957, 108 Kwidzyn residents left. In turn, between 1957 and 1959, a dozen or so Polish families arrived in the town from the Belarusian and Lithuanian SSrs148

From the 1950s until 1994, the People’s Army of Poland was stationed in the town. the soldiers inhabited both post-German barracks complexes. the barracks on Grudziądzka Street housed the Anti-tank Artillery Brigade from 1951, followed by the Anti-tank Artillery regiment and the rocket Artillery Squadron. the last unit to be stationed in this complex was the 14th Anti-tank regiment, who left Kwidzyn on 15 September 1994. the barracks on Kościuszki Street, once vacated by the Soviet army, were repurposed as a venue of the repair workshop for the state automobile transport company (PKS), which the town authorities wanted to expand and turn into a car body factory. However, this idea did not gain the approval of the head office and the workshop was closed down in 1948. From the 1960s, the barracks were occupied by the Communications Battalion and, later years, by the 24th Communications regiment, which was stationed in Kwidzyn until it was transferred to cracow on 11 September 1993. However, the administrative reports emphasised that all post-war Kwidzyn population was roman Catholic. Immediately after the war, all the Evangelical cemeteries in Kwidzyn and one Catholic cemetery were also liquidated. In the first years after the war, the deceased were buried in the former Evangelical cemetery in what is now Hallera Street. From the beginning of the 1950s, the dead were buried exclusively in the municipal cemetery on Malborska Street in Kwidzyn. An important element of the religious life of the town was the location of religious congregations. Apart from the male Franciscan order, the congregation of Benedictine nuns had its seat in Kwidzyn.

In the mid-1960s, the population of Kwidzyn’s only Catholic parish dedicated to the Holy trinity exceeded 20,000 worshippers. During the celebrations of the centenary of the construction of the church of the Holy trinity, with the decree of 5 August 1972, the bishop of Warmia, Józef Drzazga, established a new town parish of St. John the Evangelist in the former cathedral, which was cared for by the Franciscans. According to the data collected by the Department of religions of the Presidium of the WrN in Gdańsk and the Provincial Committee of the Polish united Workers’ Party (PZPr), apart from the roman Catholic community, in the religious structure of Kwidzyn there were also officially the Adventist and Methodist churches. the Methodist chapel was located on Basztowa Street. It was also used by a small number of Evangelicals, some of whom descended from the indigenous inhabitants of Kwidzyn, and those who came from Masuria as well as Baptists. the number of members of the Evangelical-Augsburg, Adventist and Baptist communities in the second half of the 1960s amounted to about 80 people150 Source: J. the area of the town in hectares was 2,182 ha. In 2006, the area was slightly adjusted and nowadays amounts to 2,154 ha. the town’s territory is divided into three parts by the railway tracks and main roads. the eastern part consists of the following housing estates Bajkowe, Piastowskie, Zatorze I and II, Nad Liwą and Zacisze. the eastern part is dominated by multi-family housing, but there is also a suburb with single-family housing. the north-western part of the town is the older, core part of the town with townhouses and multi-family houses. It comprises a historic centre and a main street routes with business premises. It includes the town centre, the old town, and two housing estates, Spółdzielcze and Hallera. Industrial plants are located in the southern part of the town. the current spatial layout of the town is invariably determined by natural (the valleys of the Vistula and Liwa rivers) and infrastructural (railway tracks, industrial district) conditions153 In terms of religion, the population was predominantly Catholic. Following political transformation in Poland, also the diocesan division was changed: the Diocese of Elbląg was erected by Pope John Paul II on 25 March 1992, and Kwidzyn was incorporated into it. the cathedral church was elevated to the status of a concathedral and then co-cathedral, and the Franciscans were transferred to the church of the Holy trinity. the number of Catholic parishes in the town increased from two to five. In addition to the church of the Holy trinity and the parish at the cathedral in Kwidzyn, other churches were built: on Słowackiego Street (church of Mercy, parish erected 10.09.1981, church 1998), Piastowska Street (St. Brother Albert, parish erected 25.04.1990, church 2012) and Sportowa Street (St. Adalbert, parish erected 21.02.1995, church 2000)154. In 1994, the Sisters of St. Elizabeth returned to Kwidzyn, previously expelled from their work at the town hospital upon the decision of the communist authorities in 1953. they moved into their previous premises on Kopernika Street, a building that since their expulsion had been used for a garrison hotel and a military kindergarten. In this building, since 2006, the sisters have been running the St. Elisabeth’s Nursing Home, mainly providing care for the elderly. A congregation of Jehovah’s Witnesses had been operating in Kwidzyn since the 1970s.

Currently, Kwidzyn is classified as a medium-sized county town, with the importance of a sub-regional centre. However, metropolisation is one of the factors determining its spatial development, which is visible in the decreasing population of Kwidzyn. In terms of the development, the town is distinguished by a very high rate of population living in multi-family housing – 85.9%,157 where the average floor area of a flat is 19.4 m2 in multi-family housing and 14 m2 in single-family housing158 Modern Kwidzyn is an industrial town, where the main economic sectors are the cellulose and paper industry, electronics, electrical engineering, woodworking, and fruit and vegetable processing. the town is home to many companies established with foreign capital. In 2013, after almost 20 years of efforts by the Kwidzyn authorities and three years of construction, a fixed bridge crossing on the Vistula became available, once again making the town accessible from the western part of Poland.
